## This tutorial

The "Diffusion and Contagion" tutorial follows states that nodes adopt or not,
such as an infection or an innovation.
This tutorial follows opinions that are numbers,
such as the probability that someone puts on a statement being true,
or their position on a scale from left to right.
Here a node does not adopt an opinion from one neighbour:
it moves its opinion towards the opinions of the nodes it listens to.

<img src="https://media.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPWVjZjA1ZTQ3bXdtbGs1azJnZWUzdGZycTRsMGg0a2twM2RxYjdveWtuNzV3eWo1MiZlcD12MV9naWZzX3NlYXJjaCZjdD1n/xjQfDCSRr2jkH3SPab/giphy.gif" alt="learn every day gif" width = "500"/>

By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- [ ] &nbsp; 'play' a DeGroot learning model over a network, and plot the result
- [ ] &nbsp; say when a network will reach a consensus, and how fast
- [ ] &nbsp; understand how stubbornness keeps disagreement alive
- [ ] &nbsp; understand bounded confidence, and the clusters of opinion it makes
- [ ] &nbsp; see how maximally diverse groups learn differently from groups of like minds
- [ ] &nbsp; understand repulsion, and how a balanced signed network polarises
- [ ] &nbsp; find the nodes with the most influence on the opinions at the end
- [ ] &nbsp; say when a crowd stays wise, when talking makes it wiser, and where misinformation does most harm
- [ ] &nbsp; show how a zealot can move the window of opinions that others will listen to
- [ ] &nbsp; tell the equilibria of these models apart, and when there is none

## Learning models

The simplest learning model is the DeGroot model.
At each step, every node takes the average of the opinions
of the nodes it listens to.
A tie from one node to another means that the first node listens to the second.
A node divides its attention among the nodes it listens to,
in proportion to the tie weights (their absolute values, for a signed network).
`to_influence()` shows these shares as a matrix.
Under DeGroot, a node does not count its own opinion,
unless the network has a tie from the node to itself.
All nodes update at once at each step,
and the ties do not change, whatever the opinions do.
A question often asked of these models is whether,
from different first opinions, the opinions converge through
(network) interaction.
A network that is strongly connected and aperiodic
converges to a consensus of (any) opinions entered.

### Expectations of convergence and consensus

Let's try this out on the `ison_networkers` dataset of communication
among network academics.
Perhaps we wish to get them to change their local networks/behaviour,
but they have different beliefs about whether this will make a difference.
To see whether this network will converge to consensus,
check whether the network is `r gloss("connected")` and `r gloss("aperiodic")`:

+ `is_connected()` marks whether every node can reach every other node.
On a directed network, it follows the direction of the ties by default (strong connectivity);
add `connectivity = "weak"` to ignore their direction.
+ `is_aperiodic()` marks whether network is aperiodic, meaning there is no integer k > 1 that divides the length of every cycle of the graph.

```{r aperiod, exercise = TRUE, purl = FALSE}

```

```{r aperiod-hint, purl = FALSE}
# By default is_connected() will check whether a directed network
# is strongly connected.
```

```{r aperiod-solution}
is_connected(ison_networkers)
is_aperiodic(ison_networkers)
```

```{r consens-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Based on these results, would you expect this network to converge to a consensus?",
  answer("No"),
  answer("Yes", correct = TRUE, message = "A strongly connected, aperiodic network will converge to a single consensus."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

```{r aperiod-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("If every component were aperiodic, but there were two or more strongly connected components, what would happen?",
  answer("There would be no convergence",
         message = "Each component still settles."),
  answer("There would be convergence to a single consensus",
         message = "Not in general: each group that listens to no one outside it settles on its own value."),
  answer("There would be convergence", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Each group that listens only to itself would reach its own consensus, and the others would end in between",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "A group that listens to no one outside it is a closed class, as in a Markov chain. Each closed class settles on its own value, and the other nodes settle on a mix of these values."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

### Playing the DeGroot learning model

Now let's see whether you are right.
We want to see whether some random distribution of beliefs converges
to a consensus in this network (`ison_networkers`).
Let's play the DeGroot learning model on this network
with a vector of random beliefs
(the same length as the nodes in the network)
drawn from the binomial distribution with **probability 0.25**.
Create the distribution of **beliefs** and graph the network
to show where they have been distributed.
Then play the learning model with `play_opinion()` and these beliefs,
and plot the result.

```{r degroot, exercise = TRUE, purl = FALSE, fig.width=9}

```

```{r degroot-hint, purl = FALSE}
beliefs <- rbinom(net_nodes(____), 1, prob = 0.25)
____ |> mutate_nodes(____ = beliefs) |> graphr(node_color = "____")
netlearn <- play_opinion(____, ____)
plot(____)
```

```{r degroot-solution}
beliefs <- rbinom(net_nodes(ison_networkers), 1, prob = 0.25)
ison_networkers |> mutate_nodes(beliefs = beliefs) |> graphr(node_color = "beliefs")
(netlearn <- play_opinion(ison_networkers, beliefs))
plot(netlearn)
```

Each line in this plot represents the belief trajectory of a single node
at each step.
About a quarter of the nodes begin believing,
and the other three quarters do not.
Then we can see how responsive these nodes are to the random distribution
of beliefs across the network.
Some revise their beliefs more significantly than others.
To see the opinion of each node at each step as a table,
use `as_opinion()`.
`play_opinion()` stops when no opinion moves by more than `tolerance`,
so the last step is very near to the end, but not exactly at it.

```{r degroot-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("What are some true statements about these results?",
  answer("Some nodes revise their beliefs more than others.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("There seems to be a consensus.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("It takes more than two steps to reach consensus.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("One node never updates their belief beyond their initial belief.",
         message = "All nodes in this network eventually update their beliefs."),
  answer("I would get the same shared belief if I reran the code.",
         message = "If you reran the code, a different random belief vector would be created and more or less influential nodes might believe or not."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE
)
```

### How fast is a consensus?

Whether a network reaches a consensus is one question;
how fast it reaches it is another.
`net_by_convergence()` from `{netrics}` measures the share of the distance
to the opinions at the end that is closed at each step, in the long run.
A value of 1 settles in one step, and a value of 0 never settles.
It needs only the network, not a played model.
Compare the networkers with a complete network of the same size (32 nodes),
and with two rings: one of 31 nodes and one of 32 nodes.

```{r convergence, exercise = TRUE, purl = FALSE}

```

```{r convergence-solution}
net_by_convergence(ison_networkers)
net_by_convergence(create_filled(32))
net_by_convergence(create_ring(31))
net_by_convergence(create_ring(32))
```

```{r convergence-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Which statements are true?",
  answer("In a complete network, every node listens to every other node, so the opinions settle almost at once.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("On a ring of 31, each node listens only to its two neighbours, so an opinion takes many steps to travel around it.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("On a ring of 32, the opinions can swing back and forth for ever, because every cycle has an even length.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Such a network is periodic, so DeGroot learning need not settle."),
  answer("A ring is not connected.",
         message = "A ring is connected: every node can reach every other node."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

## Stubbornness

In the DeGroot model, a strongly connected, aperiodic network always ends in a consensus.
But many disagreements last.
One reason is that people hold on to their first opinion.
In the Friedkin–Johnsen model,
each node has a `r gloss("stubbornness")` from 0 to 1:
how much it keeps its first opinion, compared with what the network says.
A stubbornness of 0 is DeGroot's model,
and a stubbornness of 1 is a node that never moves.
Note that a stubborn node is pulled back to its _first_ opinion,
not to the opinion it held at the last step.
That first opinion never changes.

### A path of three

Let us make the smallest example: a path A–B–C,
where A starts at 0, B at 0.5, and C at 1.
`create_explicit()` makes the path from a formula.
Play the opinions with no stubbornness,
and then with a `stubbornness` of 0.5 for every node.
Use `as_opinion()` to see the opinions at each step.

```{r path, exercise = TRUE}
path <- create_explicit(A-B-C)
graphr(path)
```

```{r path-hint, purl = FALSE}
as_opinion(play_opinion(path, c(0, 0.5, 1)))
as_opinion(play_opinion(path, c(0, 0.5, 1), stubbornness = ____))
```

```{r path-solution}
path <- create_explicit(A-B-C)
as_opinion(play_opinion(path, c(0, 0.5, 1)))
as_opinion(play_opinion(path, c(0, 0.5, 1), stubbornness = 0.5))
```

```{r path-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Where do the opinions end with a stubbornness of 0.5 for every node?",
  answer("0.25, 0.5, and 0.75", correct = TRUE,
         message = "Each end node is pulled half to B and half to its own first opinion."),
  answer("0.5, 0.5, and 0.5",
         message = "That is where they end with no stubbornness."),
  answer("0, 0.5, and 1",
         message = "That would be a stubbornness of 1, where no node moves."),
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

Note that with stubbornness the opinions still settle,
but they settle apart.
Partly stubborn nodes are enough to keep a disagreement alive.

### Stubborn networkers

Now let only the networker with the highest eigenvector centrality be stubborn,
with a stubbornness of 1,
and start them at an opinion of 1 while all others start at 0.
Then let all networkers be a little stubborn (0.1),
and compare the two plots.

```{r stubborn, exercise = TRUE, fig.width=9}

```

```{r stubborn-hint, purl = FALSE}
lead <- node_is_max(node_by_eigenvector(ison_networkers))
first <- ifelse(lead, 1, 0)
plot(play_opinion(ison_networkers, first, stubbornness = ifelse(lead, ____, 0)))
plot(play_opinion(ison_networkers, first, stubbornness = ____))
```

```{r stubborn-solution}
lead <- node_is_max(node_by_eigenvector(ison_networkers))
first <- ifelse(lead, 1, 0)
plot(play_opinion(ison_networkers, first, stubbornness = ifelse(lead, 1, 0)))
plot(play_opinion(ison_networkers, first, stubbornness = 0.1))
```

```{r stubborn-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Which statements are true?",
  answer("One fully stubborn node pulls everyone else to its first opinion.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("Where every node is a little stubborn, the opinions settle apart.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("Stubbornness stops the opinions from settling.",
         message = "The opinions still settle, but not always at one consensus."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

## Bounded confidence

Another reason that disagreements last is that people listen only to
those whose opinions are near enough to their own.
(If you have ever made excuses to leave a dinner party early, you know this model:
some people are just too different.)
These are models of `r gloss("bounded confidence")`.
`confidence` says how far apart two opinions can be
for one node still to listen to the other.
Two rules use it:

- `rule = "hegselmann_krause"`: all nodes at once take the average of the
opinions of only those nodes they listen to whose opinions are within
`confidence` of their own.
Unlike DeGroot, each node always counts its own opinion here.
This rule is deterministic.
- `rule = "deffuant"`: at each step, one node is drawn at random,
and it draws one of the nodes it listens to.
If their opinions are within `confidence`, each moves halfway towards the other.
This rule is random, and it changes only one pair at each step,
so it needs many more `steps`.

### Clusters of opinion

Draw the first opinions of the networkers at random, from 0 to 1.
Play the Hegselmann–Krause rule with a `confidence` of 0.1, and plot it.

Then see how the clusters change with the `confidence`.
`sweep_opinion()` plays the rule for each setting that you give it in `vary`,
here for each `confidence` from 0.05 to 0.5,
and counts the clusters of opinion at the end of each.
Give it 100 `steps`, so that the opinions have time to settle.

```{r hk, exercise = TRUE, fig.width=9}
set.seed(1)
first <- runif(net_nodes(ison_networkers))
```

```{r hk-hint, purl = FALSE}
plot(play_opinion(ison_networkers, first, rule = "____", confidence = ____))
hk <- sweep_opinion(ison_networkers, first, rule = "____", steps = 100,
                    vary = list(confidence = seq(____, ____, 0.05)))
```

```{r hk-solution}
set.seed(1)
first <- runif(net_nodes(ison_networkers))
plot(play_opinion(ison_networkers, first, rule = "hegselmann_krause",
                  confidence = 0.1))
hk <- sweep_opinion(ison_networkers, first, rule = "hegselmann_krause",
                    steps = 100, vary = list(confidence = seq(0.05, 0.5, 0.05)))
hk
plot(hk)
```

```{r hk-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("What does a narrower confidence do?",
  answer("It splits the opinions into more clusters, which no longer listen to each other.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("It makes the opinions reach one consensus faster.",
         message = "A wider confidence lets more nodes listen to each other."),
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

### Random encounters

Think of the Deffuant rule as a series of coffee breaks:
two colleagues meet, and if they are not too far apart, they meet in the middle.
Now play the Deffuant rule on the same first opinions,
with a `confidence` of 0.1 and 2000 `steps`.
This rule is random, so each time it is played, its result can differ.
So sweep it 10 times for each `confidence` from 0.1 to 0.5,
and set a seed in `control` so that you can repeat the result.

```{r deffuant, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "hk", fig.width=9}

```

```{r deffuant-solution}
set.seed(1)
first <- runif(net_nodes(ison_networkers))
plot(play_opinion(ison_networkers, first, rule = "deffuant",
                  confidence = 0.1, steps = 2000))
deffuant <- sweep_opinion(ison_networkers, first, rule = "deffuant",
                          steps = 2000, times = 10, control = list(seed = 2),
                          vary = list(confidence = seq(0.1, 0.5, 0.1)))
deffuant
plot(deffuant)
```

```{r deffuant-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("How does the Deffuant rule differ from the Hegselmann–Krause rule?",
  answer("Only one pair of nodes meets at each step, so it takes many more steps.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("The result can change each time it is played, unless a seed is set.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "So the plot shows a band over the 10 runs of each setting."),
  answer("It does not use `confidence`.",
         message = "Both rules use `confidence`."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

### Diverse groups

Bounded confidence also matters for how we make groups,
whether committees, seminar groups, or juries.
`node_in_roulette()` from `{netrics}` puts the nodes into groups that are
as diverse as possible on an attribute, such as their first opinions.
Let us compare such maximally diverse groups with groups of like minds,
where each group holds the nodes whose first opinions are nearest to one another.
In each group, every member listens to every other member,
which `create_components()` makes from a membership.

```{r diverse, exercise = TRUE, fig.width=9}
set.seed(1)
first <- runif(net_nodes(ison_networkers))
diverse <- node_in_roulette(ison_networkers, groups = 4,
                            attribute = first, balance = 1)
alike <- ceiling(rank(first) / 8)
diverse_groups <- create_components(32, membership = diverse)
alike_groups <- create_components(32, membership = alike)
```

```{r diverse-hint, purl = FALSE}
# Play the DeGroot model in each kind of group, and average the end by group
ends <- unlist(tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(diverse_groups, first)), 1))
tapply(ends, diverse, mean)
```

```{r diverse-solution}
set.seed(1)
first <- runif(net_nodes(ison_networkers))
diverse <- node_in_roulette(ison_networkers, groups = 4,
                            attribute = first, balance = 1)
alike <- ceiling(rank(first) / 8)
diverse_groups <- create_components(32, membership = diverse)
alike_groups <- create_components(32, membership = alike)
# DeGroot: the opinion that each group ends with
ends <- unlist(tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(diverse_groups, first)), 1))
tapply(ends, diverse, mean)
ends <- unlist(tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(alike_groups, first)), 1))
tapply(ends, alike, mean)
# Bounded confidence: the number of clusters at the end
sweep_opinion(diverse_groups, first, rule = "hegselmann_krause",
              vary = list(confidence = c(0.15, 0.3)))
sweep_opinion(alike_groups, first, rule = "hegselmann_krause",
              vary = list(confidence = c(0.15, 0.3)))
```

```{r diverse-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Which statements are true?",
  answer("With DeGroot learning, the diverse groups reach about the same conclusion as each other.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Each diverse group averages a wide range of opinions, so each ends near the mean of all."),
  answer("With DeGroot learning, the groups of like minds each keep a different conclusion.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("With bounded confidence, the diverse groups break into many clusters.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "Members of a diverse group are too far apart to listen to each other. A wider confidence brings some of them back together."),
  answer("Diversity always helps a group to agree.",
         message = "It helps only where the members listen to opinions far from their own."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

Diversity spreads the information that each group holds,
but it helps only where members listen to opinions far from their own.

## Repulsion

So far, every tie pulls a node towards the opinions of the nodes it listens to.
But we may also move away from the opinions of those we dislike:
if _they_ are for it, I must be against it.
In a signed network, a negative tie can stand for such repulsion:
the node moves towards the opposite of the other node's opinion.
Opposite opinions are then opposite signs,
so the opinions are on a scale centred on 0, from -1 to 1.

A signed network is `r gloss("structurally balanced", "balance")` where its nodes
split into two camps, with positive ties inside each camp
and negative ties between them.
Where it is balanced, repulsion splits the opinions into two camps of opposite signs.
Where it is not, the opinions are pulled towards 0.

### The road to war

`irps_wwi` holds the alliances (positive) and enmities (negative)
of six European powers from 1872 to 1918.
`to_time()` gives the network in one year.
Play the same first opinions on the network in 1890 and in 1914,
and check the balance of each with `net_by_balance()`.

```{r wwi, exercise = TRUE, fig.width=9}
first <- c(0.5, 0.2, 0.1, -0.1, -0.3, 0.4)
graphr(to_time(irps_wwi, 1914))
```

```{r wwi-hint, purl = FALSE}
as_opinion(play_opinion(to_time(irps_wwi, ____), first, steps = 500))
net_by_balance(to_time(irps_wwi, ____))
```

```{r wwi-solution}
first <- c(0.5, 0.2, 0.1, -0.1, -0.3, 0.4)
tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(to_time(irps_wwi, 1890), first, steps = 500)), 1)
net_by_balance(to_time(irps_wwi, 1890))
tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(to_time(irps_wwi, 1914), first, steps = 500)), 1)
net_by_balance(to_time(irps_wwi, 1914))
```

```{r wwi-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Why do the opinions split into two camps in 1914, but not in 1890?",
  answer("In 1914 the powers form two blocs, with alliances inside and enmities between, so the network is balanced.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("In 1914 there are more negative ties.",
         message = "The number of negative ties is not what matters, but whether they divide the network into two camps."),
  answer("In 1890 the powers had no enmities.",
         message = "Look at the ties of 1890: there are enmities, but they do not divide the powers into two camps."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

Note that only the DeGroot rule can use negative ties currently.

## Who has influence?

Where the opinions reach a consensus,
the consensus is a weighted mean of the first opinions.
The weight of each node is its influence:
`node_by_influence()` from `{netrics}` measures it.
Without stubbornness, it is the left eigenvector of the influence matrix
from `to_influence()`, where each row says whom a node listens to.
This is also called the social power of a node.
`node_by_influence()` and `node_by_opinion()` compute the exact end,
not a played one, so they need no `steps`.
If the network is periodic, the opinions swing for ever,
and these functions give the mean of the swing.

### Influence and eigenvector centrality

It is often said that the most influential nodes in a network are those
with the highest eigenvector centrality.
Compare `node_by_influence()` with `node_by_eigenvector()` for the networkers.

```{r influence, exercise = TRUE, fig.width=9}

```

```{r influence-solution}
node_by_influence(ison_networkers)
node_by_eigenvector(ison_networkers)
cor(node_by_influence(ison_networkers), node_by_eigenvector(ison_networkers))
ison_networkers |>
  mutate_nodes(influence = node_by_influence(ison_networkers)) |>
  graphr(node_size = "influence")
```

```{r influence-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Which statements are true?",
  answer("The two measures agree closely, and give the same most central node.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("The two measures can order the other nodes differently.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("The two measures are the same.",
         message = "Eigenvector centrality uses the adjacency matrix; influence uses the matrix of whom each node listens to, where each row sums to 1."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

### Free play: Networkers

Which networkers would you try to convince first,
so that the whole network comes to agree with you?
Give an opinion of 1 to the node with the highest influence and 0 to all others,
play the DeGroot model, and compare the consensus with its influence share,
`node_by_influence(ison_networkers, normalized = FALSE)`.

```{r eigen, exercise = TRUE, purl=FALSE, fig.width=9}

```

```{r eigen-hint}
who <- node_is_max(node_by_influence(ison_networkers))
ison_networkers |>
  mutate_nodes(who_to_convince = who) |>
  graphr(node_color = who_to_convince)
beliefs2 <- ifelse(who, 1, 0)
(netlearn2 <- play_opinion(ison_networkers, beliefs2))
plot(netlearn2)
node_by_influence(ison_networkers, normalized = FALSE)[who]
```

## Wisdom of crowds

Imagine that each networker makes an estimate of some true value,
for example the number of papers in a journal, with some error.
The mean of all their estimates is often close to the truth,
since the errors cancel out: the `r gloss("wisdom of crowds")`.
Francis Galton found that the crowd at a country fair guessed the weight of an ox
to within one percent, better than most of the experts there.
But what if they talk first, and then agree on one consensus?
The consensus is the mean of their first estimates,
weighted by the influence of each node.
Such a crowd stays wise
only where no node has too much influence.

### Does talking make the crowd wiser?

Let the true value be 50, and let each estimate miss it by an error
with a standard deviation of 10.
The `normalized = FALSE` influence of each node is its weight in the consensus,
so `sum(w * errors)` is the error of the consensus.
Draw the errors 1000 times for the networkers, a star, and a complete network,
and compare the spread of the error of the consensus.

One catch: a star is periodic, so its opinions would swing between the centre and the leaves for ever
(remember the rings above?).
So let every node also listen a little to itself, with `to_looped()`.
That is realistic anyway: few of us drop our own estimate entirely.

```{r wisdom, exercise = TRUE}
set.seed(1)
estimates <- 50 + rnorm(32, 0, 10)
consensus <- play_opinion(ison_networkers, estimates)
tail(as_opinion(consensus), 1)
mean(estimates)
```

```{r wisdom-hint, purl = FALSE}
w <- node_by_influence(to_looped(ison_networkers), normalized = FALSE)
max(w)
sd(replicate(1000, sum(w * rnorm(32, 0, 10))))
```

```{r wisdom-solution}
for(net in list(ison_networkers, create_star(32), create_filled(32))){
  w <- node_by_influence(to_looped(net), normalized = FALSE)
  print(c(largest_influence = max(w),
          error_of_consensus = sd(replicate(1000, sum(w * rnorm(32, 0, 10))))))
}
```

```{r wisdom-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Which crowd is the wisest after it talks?",
  answer("The complete network, because every node has the same small influence.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("The star, because the centre hears every estimate.",
         message = "The centre has about a third of all influence, so its own error counts for a third of the error of the consensus."),
  answer("All three, because they all reach a consensus.",
         message = "They all reach a consensus, but not one equally close to the truth."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

### When does talking help?

In the DeGroot model, talking cannot make the crowd wiser _on average_:
the consensus weights the estimates unequally,
and the plain mean, with equal weights, has the smallest expected error.
But in experiments, Becker, Brackbill and Centola (2017) found that
talking made crowds wiser, if their network was egalitarian:
if no node had much more influence than the others.
One reason is that people whose first estimate is near the truth
tend to revise it less.
So the accurate people are more stubborn.

Let the stubbornness of each node be 1 minus its error,
as a share of the largest error.
Then the most accurate node is a zealot, and the least accurate is not stubborn at all.
`node_by_opinion()` gives the opinion of each node at the end,
from the nodal attributes "opinions" and "stubbornness".
Compare the error of the mean before and after the nodes talk,
200 times, in a random network, a star, and the networkers,
each with `to_looped()` as before.

```{r egalitarian, exercise = TRUE}
set.seed(1)
estimates <- 50 + rnorm(32, 0, 10)
error <- abs(estimates - 50)
crowd <- to_looped(generate_random(32, 0.2)) |>
  mutate_nodes(opinions = estimates, stubbornness = 1 - error / max(error))
ends <- node_by_opinion(crowd)
c(before = abs(mean(estimates) - 50), after = abs(mean(ends) - 50))
```

```{r egalitarian-solution}
set.seed(1)
nets <- list(random = generate_random(32, 0.2), star = create_star(32),
             networkers = ison_networkers)
for(name in names(nets)){
  wiser <- replicate(200, {
    estimates <- 50 + rnorm(32, 0, 10)
    error <- abs(estimates - 50)
    crowd <- to_looped(nets[[name]]) |>
      mutate_nodes(opinions = estimates, stubbornness = 1 - error / max(error))
    ends <- node_by_opinion(crowd)
    abs(mean(ends) - 50) < abs(mean(estimates) - 50)
  })
  print(c(network = name, wiser = mean(wiser)))
}
```

```{r egalitarian-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Which statements are true?",
  answer("In the random network, the crowd is wiser after it talks more often than not.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("In the star, the crowd is wiser after it talks less often than not.",
         correct = TRUE,
         message = "The centre has most of the influence, so the crowd follows it, whether it is accurate or not."),
  answer("Where the accurate nodes are stubborn, talking always helps.",
         message = "It helps only where no node has too much influence."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

## Misinformation

What happens when some nodes spread a false opinion and never change it?
(Every group chat seems to have one.)
Such a fully stubborn node is sometimes called a `r gloss("zealot")`.
In the DeGroot model, one zealot in a strongly connected network
pulls every other node to its opinion in the end.
Where the others are also a little stubborn,
the pull is partial, and it depends on where the zealot sits.

Spreading a false claim and believing it are two different processes.
Passing a story on is a diffusion:
each node has heard the story or not,
as in the "Diffusion and Contagion" tutorial.
Believing it is learning:
how much a node believes the story moves towards what the nodes it listens to believe.
A story can reach everyone and convince no one,
or reach only a few and still shift what the whole network believes.
This section is about belief.

### Where does misinformation do most harm?

Let the truth be 0, and let the networkers start near it.
Then let one node be a zealot at 1,
and all others hold on to their first opinion with a stubbornness of 0.3.
Compare a zealot with the highest influence and one with the lowest,
by the mean opinion at the end.

```{r zealot, exercise = TRUE, fig.width=9}
set.seed(2)
first <- rnorm(32, 0, 0.1)
influence <- node_by_influence(ison_networkers)
```

```{r zealot-hint, purl = FALSE}
zealot <- which.max(influence)
opinions <- first
opinions[zealot] <- 1
stubborn <- rep(0.3, 32)
stubborn[zealot] <- ____
ends <- tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(ison_networkers, opinions,
                                     stubbornness = stubborn, steps = 500)), 1)
mean(unlist(ends))
```

```{r zealot-solution}
set.seed(2)
first <- rnorm(32, 0, 0.1)
influence <- node_by_influence(ison_networkers)
for(zealot in c(which.max(influence), which.min(influence))){
  opinions <- first
  opinions[zealot] <- 1
  stubborn <- rep(0.3, 32)
  stubborn[zealot] <- 1
  ends <- tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(ison_networkers, opinions,
                                       stubbornness = stubborn, steps = 500)), 1)
  print(c(zealot = node_labels(ison_networkers)[zealot],
          mean_opinion = round(mean(unlist(ends)), 3)))
}
```

```{r zealot-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Which statements are true?",
  answer("A zealot with more influence moves the network further from the truth.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("A zealot with little influence does almost no harm here.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("Where no other node is stubborn, a zealot has no effect.",
         message = "Where no other node is stubborn, one zealot pulls every node to its opinion in the end."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

What could stop a zealot?
Try a second zealot at the truth, 0, as a fact-checker,
and move it to different places in the network.

```{r factcheck, exercise = TRUE, exercise.setup = "zealot", fig.width=9}

```

### Moving the window

A zealot whose opinion is far from everyone else's has no pull
where people listen only to opinions near their own.
Joseph Overton described a "window" of the policies that the public will accept
at a given time.
A policy outside the window is unthinkable, whoever argues for it.
But the window can move.
In a model of bounded confidence, each node's `confidence` is such a window,
centred on its own opinion.

Let the networkers start between 0 and 0.4,
and let the node with the most influence be a zealot.
Play the Hegselmann–Krause rule with a `confidence` of 0.2.
First, let the zealot jump straight to 1.
Then let the zealot move in small steps of 0.1, from 0.3 to 1,
and let each step start from the opinions at the end of the step before.

```{r overton, exercise = TRUE, fig.width=9}
set.seed(1)
first <- runif(32, 0, 0.4)
zealot <- which.max(node_by_influence(ison_networkers))
stubborn <- ifelse(seq_len(32) == zealot, 1, 0)
```

```{r overton-hint, purl = FALSE}
# One jump
jump <- first
jump[zealot] <- 1
ends <- tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(ison_networkers, jump, rule = "hegselmann_krause",
                                     confidence = ____, stubbornness = stubborn,
                                     steps = 100)), 1)
mean(unlist(ends)[-zealot])

# Small steps
opinions <- first
for(step in seq(0.3, 1, ____)){
  opinions[zealot] <- step
  opinions <- unlist(tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(ison_networkers, ____,
                                                  rule = "hegselmann_krause",
                                                  confidence = 0.2,
                                                  stubbornness = stubborn,
                                                  steps = 100)), 1))
  print(c(zealot = step, others = round(mean(opinions[-zealot]), 2)))
}
```

```{r overton-solution}
set.seed(1)
first <- runif(32, 0, 0.4)
zealot <- which.max(node_by_influence(ison_networkers))
stubborn <- ifelse(seq_len(32) == zealot, 1, 0)
# One jump
jump <- first
jump[zealot] <- 1
ends <- tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(ison_networkers, jump, rule = "hegselmann_krause",
                                     confidence = 0.2, stubbornness = stubborn,
                                     steps = 100)), 1)
mean(unlist(ends)[-zealot])
# Small steps
opinions <- first
for(step in seq(0.3, 1, 0.1)){
  opinions[zealot] <- step
  opinions <- unlist(tail(as_opinion(play_opinion(ison_networkers, opinions,
                                                  rule = "hegselmann_krause",
                                                  confidence = 0.2,
                                                  stubbornness = stubborn,
                                                  steps = 100)), 1))
  print(c(zealot = step, others = round(mean(opinions[-zealot]), 2)))
}
```

```{r overton-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Which statements are true?",
  answer("A zealot that jumps to 1 is outside every window, so no one moves.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("A zealot that moves in small steps stays inside the window, and the window follows it.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("The others end at 1 because they are stubborn.",
         message = "Only the zealot is stubborn here. The others follow because each step is within their confidence."),
  random_answer_order = TRUE,
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

So an opinion that no one will hear today can become acceptable tomorrow,
if the opinions in between are heard first.
Try a wider or a narrower `confidence`, or larger steps.
How large can a step be before the window stops following?

## Equilibria and disequilibria

Each model in this tutorial settles in its own way, or does not settle at all:

| Outcome | What gives it | Where we saw it |
|---|---|---|
| Consensus | A strongly connected, aperiodic network, with no stubbornness | DeGroot on `ison_networkers` |
| Lasting disagreement | Stubbornness, which pulls each node back to its first opinion | The path A–B–C |
| Fragmentation | Bounded confidence, which cuts the ties between distant opinions | Hegselmann–Krause and Deffuant |
| Polarisation | Repulsion on a balanced signed network | `irps_wwi` in 1914 |
| Capture | One zealot in a network with no other stubborn node | Misinformation |
| No equilibrium | A periodic network, where opinions can swing for ever | A ring with an even number of nodes |

The last is a `r gloss("disequilibrium", "periodic")`.
On a ring of four nodes, each node averages its two neighbours.
Start with opinions of 1, 0, 1, and 0,
and see what happens at each step.
Then try a ring of five, with 1, 0, 1, 0, and 0.

```{r swing, exercise = TRUE}

```

```{r swing-solution}
as_opinion(play_opinion(create_ring(4), c(1, 0, 1, 0), steps = 6))
is_aperiodic(create_ring(4))
as_opinion(play_opinion(create_ring(5), c(1, 0, 1, 0, 0), steps = 50))
is_aperiodic(create_ring(5))
```

```{r swing-interp, echo = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
question("Why do the opinions on the ring of four never settle?",
  answer("Every cycle of the ring of four has an even length, so the opinions swap between the two halves at each step.",
         correct = TRUE),
  answer("The ring of four is not connected.",
         message = "It is connected, but it is not aperiodic."),
  answer("The opinions are too far apart.",
         message = "The DeGroot rule has no bounded confidence."),
  allow_retry = TRUE)
```

A real group may still settle on such a network,
because people also listen to themselves.
A self-weight, a self-loop in the network, breaks the swing.
Try `play_opinion(to_looped(create_ring(4)), c(1, 0, 1, 0))`,
and see `to_influence()` for how the self-weight is set.

## Glossary

Where opinions end up depends on whom each node listens to, and how much.
In the DeGroot model, a network that is strongly connected and aperiodic
always reaches a consensus, and how fast it gets there depends on its structure.
Stubbornness keeps a disagreement alive,
because each node is pulled back towards its first opinion.
Bounded confidence breaks a group into clusters of opinion,
since nodes stop listening to opinions too far from their own,
so diverse groups learn from one another only where their members listen widely.
Repulsion on a balanced signed network polarises opinions into two camps.
The nodes with the most influence on the end are close to,
but not the same as, those with the highest eigenvector centrality.
Talking can make a crowd wiser, but only where no node has too much influence,
and a zealot does most harm where it has most influence.
A zealot too far from the others is not heard,
but one that moves in small steps can move the whole window of acceptable opinions.
Finally, not every network settles:
on a periodic network, opinions can swing for ever.

Here are some of the terms that we have covered in this module:

`r print_glossary()`

### Next: Modelling with ERGMs

In this tutorial and the last, the network was given,
and we asked what spreads or settles on it.
But ties also form for reasons,
for example because people choose others with opinions like their own.
The "Modelling with ERGMs" tutorial models the ties themselves,
with exponential random graph models.
